book: 022 - The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless

chapters.file: ch03 - Popular Culture and Philosophy Series Editor George A. Reisch.md
ch05 - A New Lease of Life for the Undead.md
chapters.relation: The editors' introduction surveys the twenty-first-century vampire and zombie boom (Twilight, True Blood, Zombieland, Fido, Pride and Prejudice and Zombies, Humans Versus Zombies, zombie walks) and asks why zombies specifically fascinate us. It proposes that the vampire embodies a Nietzschean super-humanity beyond good and evil, still charged with unheeded guilt, while the zombie is sub-Nietzschean: a Spinozan force of decomposition, a completely non-moral interaction of matter with other matter. Zombies work as hyperdead memento mori through which we imagine our own annihilation and our transformation into something posthuman, even as they are repackaged as one more consumer product distracting us from the very Real they reflect.

chapters.file: ch06 - PART I - It’s Alive (Sort Of).md
ch07 - Not to Put Too Fine a Point on It.md
chapters.relation: Richard Greene asks why becoming Undead is bad for the one who becomes Undead and why we rank it worse than death, restricting himself to unfriendly vampires and zombies (setting aside soulful exceptions like Angel, Spike, Louis, and Ed from Shaun of the Dead). He tests Nagel's deprivation view (vampires gain infinite experiences, so nothing is deprived) and Williams's desire-frustration view (undeath replaces rather than frustrates desires: scotch for blood, pork roast for raw flesh), then Mill's better-Socrates-dissatisfied comparison and the thought that the Undead's evil nature makes undeath objectively bad. Each fails, so he concludes undeath is not objectively bad, only comparatively bad, and one might as well make the best of it.

William Larkin uses Romero's films - Karen Cooper devouring her father in Night of the Living Dead, Roger begging Peter to shoot him in Dawn, Riley's 'Those people are all dead' in Land - to argue that persons are res corporealis, bodily continuers, rather than Descartes's res cogitans. Our terror of becoming a zombie ourselves and our grief at recognized neighbors in the horde reveal that deep down we think persons survive as corpses, so bodily continuity suffices for identity while psychological continuity is unnecessary. The Locke-style body-switching intuition (prince and cobbler) that supports the psychological approach is dismissed as theoretically biased data compared to what good zombie fiction draws out of us.

Hamish Thompson asks why we kill zombies with so few qualms and whether zombification releases us from obligations to the person who was, testing brain-death criteria, altered-identity and self-defense justifications against Shaun of the Dead (Shaun's mother and Ed), Day of the Dead's Bub, White Zombie, and Invasion of the Body Snatchers. He borrows Hume's bundle theory - the self as a fiction, a bundle of perceptions rather than an essence - and Parfit's degrees of psychological continuity to dissolve the sharp alive/dead and same-person/other-person dichotomies that make zombie-killing easy. The payoff is that we are already partly zombie (Shaun's checkout line, Ed on the sofa, the author's all-night gaming), differing only in our capacity for brief autonomous, goal-directed choices like Shaun's three-plan montage.

Manuel Vargas argues the Undead are not a natural kind but a nominal kind - vampires, zombies, and composite creatures like Frankenstein's monster share nothing except our classificatory practice - and that most actual Undead would probably be of natural origin (viruses, viroids, seeds, cryonics cases) rather than supernatural. He distinguishes philosophical zombies (Chalmers's conscious-less duplicates) from genuinely Undead beings, then defines malevolent evil as acting on a non-instrumental desire to harm others. On that definition zombies (mere appetite, like a deadly virus) and even vampires (whose damnation, contrary to early Buffy, need not add malicious motives) probably lack it, so if we ever meet the Undead they would be less likely to be evil than any random living person.

chapters.file: ch11 - Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep.md
chapters.relation: Larry Hauser stages the philosophy-of-mind zombie debate through Blade Runner's Replicants: Descartes's animal automata and his hats-and-coats worry about other minds, Turing's universal machines grounding functionalism, Kripke's necessity of scientific identifications (water is necessarily H2O), and Searle's silicon-chip replacement scenario show how zombies 'eat' behaviorist, functionalist, and identity-theoretic accounts of mind. He then deploys his own 'good zombies' - the beloved who might be a zombie, super-smart NEXUS 9s, venerable zombie thinkers - to block the dualist retreat on the cognitive side of the mind. The essay closes by doubting, with Chalmers's phenomenal zombies in view, that such zombies are coherently conceivable after all, and asks whether Deckard has been 'retiring' persons like Rachel all along.

chapters.file: ch12 - PART II - Undead White Males.md
ch13 - Heil Heidegger Dracula’s Willing Executioners.md
chapters.relation: Adam Barrows reads Stoker's Dracula through Being and Time: the staking of Lucy is the liberation of a true humanity trapped in a deathless shell, and Dracula's endless, mirror-less, selfless existence is Heideggerian inauthenticity - the 'they' that tranquilizes the dying, Renfield's seduction repeating the neighbors' comforting, the refusal of being-toward-death - so vampire-hunting becomes a philosophical task of enforcing authentic, death-claiming being. The chapter then turns the critique on Heidegger himself: his Nazi membership and fundamental ontology's contempt for the everyday leave a gap for racial purity thinking, making Van Helsing's 'butcher work' look like the ritual expulsion of the inauthentic from ontological purity, and asking whether, in adaptation after adaptation, we are Dracula's willing executioners.

chapters.file: ch14 - “Hey, Let’s Get the Stuff We Need!” Putting the Mall in Its Place.md
chapters.relation: Matthew Walker reads Dawn of the Dead through Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics and Politics: the survivors' mall orgy curdles into boredom ('What have we done to ourselves?'), illustrating pleonexia, the graspingness for more than one's share of the goods of fortune that Aristotle roots in an unlimited desire for mere living - which may even explain why Romero's dead return, grasping from beyond the grave for more un-death. Aristotle's dismissal of the life of enjoyment as fit for cattle, his account of eudaimonia as the life in which our rational capacities flourish, and his defense of acquisition bounded by the good life explain why unlimited consumption zombifies the living, and why Peter and Fran must finally leave the mall empty-handed.

K. Silem Mohammad explains the horror of zombie slowness through Freud's uncanny - the return of the repressed, from White Zombie's hypnotized slaves (a figure for alienated industrial labor) to Romero's shuffling radioactive ghouls - then rebuilds undeath on Spinoza's Ethics: death as a body's parts acquiring a different proportion of motion and rest, the mind as a 'spiritual automaton,' and (via Deleuze's ethology of composition, decomposition, and bad encounters) zombies as bodies that decompose living bodies and recompose them as zombie bodies, replacing moral good and evil with good and bad. The fast zombies of 28 Days Later and the Dawn remake abandon hunger and the uncanny for pure rage and 'the Real,' signaling a late-capitalist permanent crisis in which the living have had their chance and blown it.

chapters.file: ch16 - PART III - Dirty Rotting Scoundrels.md

chapters.relation: Dale Jacquette distinguishes Hollywood zombies from Chalmers-style philosophical zombies, imagines a smiley-face birthmark that makes the latter visible, and argues that since zombies lack consciousness, pain, and intention, they are amoral - so zombie gladiatorial games would wrong no one, an improvement on the Roman munera Seneca condemned as pure murder. The thought experiment then turns on itself: even with zombie-only upbringing, screened audiences, and everything short of actual suffering on the zombies' side, the games would still be wrong for what they symbolically enact - the social condoning of slaughter of genetically human beings for entertainment. The conclusion is that consciousness and personhood do not exhaust morality: zombies get a moral pass, while the entire moral burden falls on the conscios who organize and watch.

chapters.file: ch18 - Universal Rights Vampires, Space Aliens, Robots, and Humans.md
chapters.relation: John Draeger asks which Undead can be held accountable for bloodthirsty behavior: Romero's zombies are amoral, like a poisonous plant or Cleckley's empathy-free psychopath Milt, while Dracula meticulously plans his move to London and so passes the cognitive test. Stoker's narcissistic Count stays amoral, but Coppola's Dracula (who warns Mina of her curse), Rice's guilt-torn Louis, and the self-deceiving, cruelty-enjoying Lestat show empathy, self-control, and moral reflection, making them immoral and responsible - which entitles vampires to due process rather than Van Helsing's vigilantism, to punishment aimed at rehabilitation, and to equal rights including civic participation and marriage, since the same standard would govern space aliens, robots, and humans.

Wayne Yuen argues vampires are moral agents - rational by Aristotle's standard of practical wisdom (Lestat's investments and his judgments about evildoers tasting better) and free despite their blood-craving, since craving is a strong preference, not the compulsion of the heroin addict or the castaway drinking seawater. Since animal blood is a viable alternative (Louis's rats, Angel and Spike's butcher's blood), the justifications for drinking human blood - taste, reaching full potential, spiritual peace - all fail against the principle that a world with less unnecessary suffering is better. Then the consistency argument turns on us: factory-farmed meat inflicts unnecessary suffering for the sake of taste while vegetarianism is fully viable, so condemning vampires while eating chicken is inconsistent - we as human beings are vampiric.

Robert Arp models the vampire's ontology with substance versus property dualism - Rice's vampires whose souls outlast the stake versus Blade's vampires who perish with their bodies - and uses Mill's distinction between lower bodily and higher mental pleasures from Utilitarianism to explain how vampires can both feel nothing bodily and suffer mentally (the opening quotation's regret at missing the wind in one's hair). Their real plight is the hedonistic paradox: pleasure pursued for its own sake yields pain, mistaken pleasures (Lestat on the dead twins, Blade's rave), or the boredom of an immortality that has 'seen it all.' The good guy vampires from Barnabas Collins to St. Germain escape by pursuing higher pleasures and activities for their own sake, vindicating Mill's closing advice that only those whose minds are fixed on something other than their own happiness find it.

holes.name: Natural Kinds vs Nominal Kinds
holes.what: The distinction between kinds whose membership is fixed by the world's own structure (water, electrons) and kinds unified only by our definitions and classificatory practices.
holes.why: Chapter 10's ontology of the Undead turns on arguing that vampires, zombies, and composite Undead form a merely nominal kind rather than a natural one, which grounds its claim that they share no deep unity.

holes.name: Malevolent Evil (non-instrumental desire to harm)
holes.what: A restrictive sense of evil defined by having and acting on non-instrumental motives to damage others' welfare, distinct from ordinary moral wrongdoing and from the Problem of Evil.
holes.why: Chapter 10 argues that zombies and most vampires lack exactly this motive structure and so are not evil, despite their horror-movie portrayal, making the concept the chapter's key analytical tool.

holes.name: The Amoral Psychopath (Cleckley)
holes.what: Hervey Cleckley's profile of the psychopath as cognitively normal but lacking basic empathic concern, and therefore amoral rather than immoral and not a fit target of blame.
holes.why: Chapter 18 uses Cleckley's case of Milt to draw the line between amoral creatures (Romero's zombies, Stoker's Dracula) that can be stopped but not blamed, and accountable ones (Coppola's Dracula, Louis, Lestat).
